title: Generating in the Limit with Infinitely Many Hallucinations
claim: Results across a grid of constraint settings are organized in one table, showing new bounds fill gaps left by existing ones.
layout: 2x4 grid, rows by novelty type, columns by tail precision and exhaustion; color-coded cells
description: A table-like grid of eight colored cells. Two bold header groups sit on top: 'Perfect tail precision' and 'Relaxed tail precision'. Each group has two sub-columns, 'Partial' and 'Full'. Two row labels run down the left side, rotated: 'Novelty' on top and 'γ-Novelty' below. Each cell contains a pair of math bounds, precision π̂ equal to 1 and a recall ρ̂ bound such as ≥ α/2, ≥ 1/2, ≥ max(1−β, α/3), ≥ α or = 1. Below the bounds is a theorem or corollary reference. Existing results from Kleinberg & Wei sit in lavender-blue cells, and new results marked '(ours)' sit in light green cells. The new results fill most of the bottom row and one top-row cell. The eye goes first to the green and blue color split.
caption: Overview of precision (bπ∗) and recall (bρ∗) bounds across settings defined by three constraints: novelty fraction with γ ∈[0, 1) vs. novelty, partial vs. full adversarial exhaustion, and perfect tail precision (bτ∗(T, G) = 1) vs. relaxed tail precision (bτ∗(T, G) can be 0). Existing results are in blue and new results in green. T is the target language and T is an enumeration of T. The adversary reveals a language A ⊆T via an exhaustion A. The learner outputs a guess language G via the exhaustion G. In the full exhaustion setting, the adversary is restricted to revealing full exhaustions; in the partial setting, it may reveal a partial exhaustion. A is characterized by lower and upper recall bounds bρ∗(T , A) ≥α and bρ∗(T , A) ≤β.
abstract: The classic paradigm of language identification in the limit models learning as a game between an adversary, who reveals strings from an unknown target language, and a learner tasked with identifying that language. The recently introduced framework of language generation in the limit shifted the objective to better reflect modern language modeling, requiring the learner to produce valid, unseen strings from the target language. Related work highlighted a fundamental tension: a broad coverage of the target often comes at the cost of validity. We introduce a new notion of precision and recast this problem as the classic recall-precision trade-off. We analyze generation in the limit under varying constraints on enumeration, novelty, and validity, aimed at reflecting settings closer to those encountered by large language models. A key contribution is our analysis of learners that are not eventually valid: we allow infinitely many mistakes, provided their frequency tends to zero so that precision remains one. We show that this relaxation can strictly increase recall when the adversary permanently withholds a large portion of the target language. We also study a continuous relaxation of the novelty constraint that requires only a fixed fraction of outputs to be novel. Taken together, our results move toward a more realistic model of language generation where occasional errors and repetitions are unavoidable, but their rates are controlled.
